sections.COMMENTS:
An over 1,000 km-long contractional belt runs along the eastern margin of the Adriatic Sea from the Alpine domain (to the North) to the Kefallonia-Lefkada Fault (to the south). The various part of this fold-and-thrust belt are known, from north to south, as Dinarides, Albanides and Hellenides and result from the continental collision between the European and African plates. Along this margin the SW-NE convergence between the two plates exhibits a strain rate of ~30 nanostrain/y (Hollenstein et al., 2003; Serpelloni et al., 2005).
Seismicity mostly concentrates in the Albanides and Hellenides. The outer portion of these chains is partly located offshore and characterized by a number of thrust fronts that all appear to be currently active. The available focal mechanisms indicate a SW-NE maximum horizontal stress axis (Papazachos et al., 1999); reverse faulting dominates, even if some smaller strike-slip events are occasionally recorded (Vannucci et al., 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006).
We propose that this Source lies on one of the outermost thrust fronts that characterize the southernmost portion of the continental collision between the African and European plates.
This Composite Source is presently characterized by shallow seismicity with many 4<M<5 events. Several large events (up to M=6.8) are also known from historical catalogues. Its average strike and rake computed by Papazachos et al. (1999) from focal mechanisms are consistent with plate motion vectors derived from GPS data and with the orientation of the thrust front reported by many investigators. Its dip was inferred from focal mechanisms (Global CMT catalogue) and from the average dip of the thrust faults detected on seismic profiles acquired for hydrocarbon exploration (e.g., Graham Wall et al., 2006).
We used GPS data to estimate the slip rate.

pictures.t: Tectonic map of the Adriatic Sea and surrounding regions
pictures.c: This tectonic scheme is the result of the interpretation of several seismic lines all over the Southern Adriatic Sea. The edge of the Mesozoic carbonate platform is also shown (from Argnani et al. [1996]).

pictures.t: Tectonic map of the Albanides and geologic cross-section
pictures.c: This map and the associated profile show the tectonic style of the Albanides fold-and-thrust belt (from Graham Wall et al. [2006]).

pictures.t: Moment tensor solution for the Adriatic Sea and surrounding regions
pictures.c: This map shows that moment tensor solutions for the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea indicate mainly reverse faulting (from Pondrelli et al. [2006]).

pictures.t: Seismicity of map Albania and adjacent regions
pictures.c: The Northern Albania and Southern Albania offshore source areas fall in the region named PL (Periadriatic Lowland) and IC (Ionian Coast), respectively (from Aliaj et al. [2004]).
Parameters of the ten seismic source zones proposed by Aliaj et al. [2004] for Albania (from Aliaj et al. [2004]).

pictures.t: Stress field map of the Aegean region and surroundings
pictures.c: This map shows the horizontal compression and tension axes all over the Aegean and surrounding regions. The stress axes adopted for the Southern Albania offshore source area are marked as A3 (from Papazachos et al. [1999]).

pictures.t: Regional cross-sections across the Po Plain and the northern Adriatic Sea
pictures.c: Interpreted regional seismic reflection profiles straddling the full extents of the Adriatic basin, including the Po Plain and the adjacent Northern Apennines (to the west), Southern Alps (to the north), and Dinarides (to the east) (from Fantoni and Franciosi [2009]).
